newsitem.title: USA: Clinton confers on Mideast peace impasse.
newsitem.headline: Clinton confers on Mideast peace impasse.

text.p: Frustrated by the Middle East negotiating impasse and concerned about mounting violence in the region, President Bill Clinton conferred with his chief Mideast diplomatic troubleshooter on Monday in preparation for a meeting with King Hussein of Jordan on Tuesday.

Ambassador Dennis Ross returned to Washington on Saturday after talks with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu aimed at keeping the latest tensions between them from derailing the 6-year-old peace process between Israel and the Palestinians.
Asked if Ross had failed in his mission, White House spokesman Mike McCurry said: "No, he did not come home empty handed, but there's a lot of hard work to do."

McCurry said Israel and the Palestinians were still "not talking to each other directly," but said one good sign was "that the Palestinian authority over the weekend moved very swiftly to head off protests that might have become violent."
"We continue to encourage both sides to recognise the utility of dialogue," Clinton's spokesman said.

Israeli-Palestinian talks have been frozen since Netanyahu two weeks ago broke ground for new Jewish settlements in Arab East Jerusalem, triggering West Bank violence that continued on Monday for a 12th staight day. Palestinians say the Har Homa project violates an Oslo peace accords commitment to decide Jerusalem's future in final status negotiations.
The crisis deepened following a March 20 suicide bombing at a Tel Aviv cafe that killed three Israelis. Israel accused Arafat of giving a tacit "green light" for militant attacks.

On Sunday night, Arab foreign ministers agreed at a Cairo meeting to recommend that their countries suspend normal ties with the Jewish state, restore an economic boycott, close down Israeli diplomatic missions and withdraw from multilateral peace talks until Israel shows greater flexibility.

McCurry sought to avoid giving crisis overtones to Clinton's meeting with Hussein, which was postponed from March 18 after an apparently deranged Jordanian soldier killed seven Israeli schoolgirls near the Jordan-Israel border.

The meeting is the fourth in a series with Middle East leaders, including Netanyahu, Arafat and Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak, over the past two months designed to give the peace process new impetus even before the latest difficulties.
"It will be working visit. It's not as formal an occasion as we have with some other foreign leaders," he said.

But another White House official said Clinton wanted to explore Hussein's ideas for reviving the peace process. He also predicted Clinton would publicly single out Hussein's on-bended-knee request for forgiveness from the families of the murdered schoolgirls as the kind of "personal reaching across the divide" needed to restore momentum to negotiations.

The official, who spoke on condition he not be identified, said Clinton and other top administration officials were frustrated by the repeated setbacks to the peace process in recent months but determined to press on.

Asked if the United States believed the hardline Netanyahu was fully committed to the peace process, the official replied after a pause: "We know he believes the peace process is the best track for improving the security of the Israeli people."

He also said Clinton was unlikely to exert the kind of pressure brought to bear on Israel by former President George Bush and his Secretary of State James Baker, who once publicly advised a previous hardline Israeli government to telephone the White House when it was serious about negotiating.
"I don't think President Clinton sees that as a productive way to do this," the official said.
